Need searches first.# Psalm 80: Verse-by-verse research notes

**What I found:** Most of the material comes from older commentaries collected on biblehub, studylight and blueletterbible (Spurgeon, Matthew Henry, Calvin, Gill, Barnes, Maclaren, Pulpit, Cambridge), plus Enduring Word (David Guzik) and Augustine on newadvent.

**What's missing:** I couldn't read the NET Bible notes, an Orthodox source, a Lutheran or Pentecostal site writing in its own voice, or anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm. Those are left out.

**Debated questions:** The Protestant disagreements are on v. 3/7/19 (what "restore/turn us" means) and v. 15/17 (who the "son" and the "man at Your right hand" are). The notes on those verses are fuller.

---

**Title / setting**
- Barnes says we can't know for certain when or why the psalm was written. It can be best explained on the supposition that it refers to the desolations caused by the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-80.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown think instead that this Psalm probably relates to the captivity of the ten tribes, as the former to that of Judah. They read "Eduth" as Testimony, referring to the topic as a testimony of God to His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-1.htm
- Spurgeon thinks the writer was probably a later Asaph. If by the Asaph of David's day, this Psalm was written in the spirit of prophecy, for it sings of times unknown to David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- Catholic (Augustine): The song here is of the Advent of the Lord and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of His vineyard. He takes the psalm as a whole to be about Christ and the Church: Head and Body, Shepherd and flock. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm (Augustine's Latin Bible numbers this psalm 79; the page cites it that way.)

**v. 1**
- Guzik, quoting Boice: God as Israel's shepherd appears in the Psalter only here and in Psalm 23. Spurgeon adds that "The name is full of tenderness, and hence is selected by the troubled Psalmist." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- Ellicott: "dwellest" should be "sittest (enthroned)." The picture comes from the throne held up by the carved cherubim in the Temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-1.htm
- Calvin (Reformed): the mercy-seat was a pledge of God's presence. The verse calls the northern tribes back from the worship set up at Dan and Bethel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html
- Augustine: the cherubim mean "fullness of knowledge." A believer can become God's seat too, because love is the fulfilment of the Law. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 2**
- Spurgeon: the three tribes were closely related, all from Rachel's line. They were wont to march together in the wilderness, following immediately behind the ark. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- Cambridge Bible: "before Ephraim" means God placing Himself at their head as a victorious leader, as He did in the wilderness. Barnes takes the three tribes to stand for the whole nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-2.htm
- Maclaren: Joseph and Benjamin had the same mother. To the psalmist's faith, the split between their descendants was temporary and unnatural. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
- Augustine reads the names as meanings: Ephraim is "fruit-bearing," Benjamin "son of the right hand," Manasseh "one forgetful." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 3 (the refrain; also vv. 7, 19)**
- Widely agreed: "make Your face shine" echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-3.htm
- Guzik: what Israel needed most was not better circumstances but God's presence and favour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- **Where Protestant teachers really differ: is "turn us" about conversion or about restoring the nation?**
  - **Conversion by God's grace.** Matthew Henry says the psalmist prays earnestly for converting grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_080.cfm
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) says the prayer shows turning was not in their power, but must be effected by the grace of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-3.htm
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) says the best turn is not that of circumstances but of character. He calls conversion as divine a work as creation, and says backsliders need God to turn them again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/80.htm
  - **Restoring the nation.** Calvin (Reformed) takes the plain meaning: "Restore us to our former state." He mentions the reading about regeneration but finds it too refined. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html
  - Barnes also says the idea is not "turn us from our sins" but simply "bring us back; restore us." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-80.html
  - Maclaren says the prayer is neither for return from exile nor for spiritual renewal. It simply asks for the return of the glories of ancient days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
  - **Bringing back exiles?** The Pulpit Commentary takes it as bringing exiles home (2 Kings 15:29). Keil & Delitzsch disagree: the people are still in their own land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-3.htm
  - Catholic (Augustine): "convert us," because You covered Your face, and we were sick: illumine Thou the same, and we shall be whole. He links God's hidden face to Christ's divinity veiled in flesh. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm
- **Revival.** Spurgeon preached this refrain as the two things revival needs: our turning to God and God's shining face. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-80.html

**v. 4**
- Maclaren (quoted by Guzik): "be angry" is a weak rendering. The Hebrew says 'wilt Thou smoke?' https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- Maclaren also says "How long?" is not impatience but hope deferred, still holding on to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
- Matthew Henry gives possible reasons God might be angry with His people's prayers. Their aims may be wrong, they may be holding on to a secret sin, or God may be testing their patience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-1.htm
- Calvin: those who pray should not settle into this feeling. They should hold against it the judgment of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html
- Augustine: God is angry as a father correcting, not as a judge condemning (Heb. 12:6). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 5**
- Coffman: the "bread of tears" points to the extreme suffering Israel was going through when the psalm was written. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-80.html
- Calvin: we share the same sins, but God gave this prayer to a nearly desperate people, so it gives us hope and keeps us praying. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html
- Augustine: "in measure" means suffering suited to our strength (1 Cor. 10:13), meant to instruct us, not crush us. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 6**
- Maclaren sums up vv. 4–6 as an angry God, a weeping nation, and mocking foes, a trilogy of woe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
- Augustine applies "a contradiction to our neighbours" to the apostles preaching the risen Christ to the Gentiles. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 7**
- Barnes: adding "of hosts" shows greater earnestness, appealing to God as leader of armies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-80.html
- Calvin: the repetition is not vain. It is meant to help the people get past every obstacle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html

**v. 8**
- Maclaren: the Exodus was the transplanting, and the defeat of the Canaanites was clearing the weeds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
- Ellicott: the verb is used both for gardening and for breaking camp. Pulpit and Cambridge suggest Genesis 49:22 ("Joseph is a fruitful vine") may lie behind the picture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-8.htm
- Spurgeon: Egypt was "unfriendly soil." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- Calvin: calling Israel a vine shows the high place God gave this people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html

**v. 9**
- Spurgeon: Canaan was cleared like a plot readied for a vineyard. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- Augustine sees "a way You have made before her" as Christ, the Way (John 14:6). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 10**
- Spurgeon: a better rendering has the vine covering the cedars. It is a picture of Israel at its best, as in Solomon's time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- Augustine: the "mountains" are the prophets, shaded because they spoke in types and figures. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: the vine reached from the Mediterranean to the Euphrates under David and Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- Augustine reads "to the River" as the Jordan. He sees it as the first stage, and the Church spreading "from sea to sea" as the vineyard's completion. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801080.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: vineyards had thorny hedges, and God Himself broke them down to discipline Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- Coffman reads "walls" as the walls of Jerusalem, already destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-80.html
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon applies the verse to the Church: where are the prophets, apostles and pastors who once guarded the vine? https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm

**v. 13**
- Maclaren: the parallel lines rule out the boar meaning one particular enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch disagree: the poet does have a nation in mind. They note the Midrash reads the boar as Edom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-8.htm
- Biblehub's study notes say the "boar" is the same unclean animal Antiochus IV later used in 167 BC. Here, though, it simply pictures devastation. https://biblehub.com/psalms/80.htm

**v. 14**
- Spurgeon: Turn thyself to us as well as us to thee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/80.htm
- Maclaren: this verse echoes the refrain, now asking God Himself to "turn." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik): restoration can come only as God turns the people back to Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/

**v. 15**
- Barnes: the Hebrew word may be a verb, "protect what Your right hand planted." "Branch" is literally "son," meaning the vine's shoots. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-15.htm
- Cambridge: the Targum reads "Messiah the king" here, but the primary reference is obviously to the nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-15.htm
- The NET Bible translates "the shoot you made to grow." https://biblehub.com/psalms/80-15.htm
- Bible.org (Utley) notes the word "shoot" may connect to the messianic "Branch" passages (Isa. 11:1; Jer. 23:5). https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-80

**v. 16**
- Guzik: the destruction came from God's own rebuke. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- Calvin: the Israelites had abandoned true religion yet were still part of the Church. They are a warning against ingratitude. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html
- Maclaren: this verse breaks into the prayer like an outcrop of lava. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm

**v. 17 (the main debated verse)**
- **Ultimately Christ:**
  - Guzik (enduringword): perhaps the reigning king first, but ultimately the Man of God's Right Hand is Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1:20, Hebrews 8:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
  - Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist): The only person who can be said to be at the right hand of God as intercessor, is JESUS the MESSIAH. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/psalms/80-17.html
  - Gill (Baptist): reads it entirely of Christ. The prayer is that God's justice would fall on Christ as surety rather than on the vine. He holds that the NT title "Son of Man" comes from here and Daniel 7:13. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-17.htm
  - An older writer quoted by Spurgeon says the immediate reference may be the king of Judah, but it must ultimately and most properly intend Jesus Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
  - Coffman says the words "Son of Man" rule out Barnes's view that this is the king of northern Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/80-15.html
- **The reigning king:** Matthew Henry says the "vine-dresser," whichever Davidic king it was, while noting that many Jewish and Christian interpreters apply it to the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/80-17.html
- **Israel itself:**
  - Maclaren: Israel, not an individual, is the "man of Thy right hand," perhaps playing on Benjamin, "son of the right hand." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm
  - Cambridge: it repeats v. 15 without the metaphor. Pulpit: Israel, or Ephraim in particular. Geneva Bible: the people as "one man or one body." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-17.htm
  - Poole: leans toward Israel, since the same words are used of the vine in v. 15. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/psalms-80.html
  - Constable: the present generation as "God's son," a wordplay on Benjamin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/80-17.html
- **Lutheran:** Barnes reports that Luther translated this as "Let thy hand guard the folks of thy right hand," taking it of the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/80-17.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** applies the words to the vine-branch, Israel. His editors note it is highly probable, that the phraseology here employed contains a mystic allusion to the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/80-17.html Another note quoted in his commentary even suggests Cyrus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-80.html
- **Translation:** the NET Bible renders the verse "the one you have chosen." https://biblehub.com/psalms/80-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Spurgeon: It is in Christ that we abide faithful; because he lives we live also. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon sees here the perseverance of the saints, grounded in Christ being enough. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps080.cfm
- VanGemeren (quoted by Guzik): only the Lord can revive, through forgiveness and renewal of the covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-80/
- Maclaren: the wise will both promise faithfulness and ask for continual help, since only God's quickening opens their lips to call on Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/80.htm

**v. 19**
- The way God is addressed rises through the three refrains: "God," then "God of hosts," then "LORD (Jehovah) God of hosts." Henry, Spurgeon and Maclaren all point this out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_080.cfm
- Barnes calls the refrain the sum and the burden of the psalm. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-80.html
- The Restoration Commentary: God will turn to Israel when Israel turns to God. The change needed is in the vine, not in God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-80.html
